subtitle: Words in apposition, and the whole system of modal verbs
words.intro: An antique dealer’s whole trade is in a single grammatical form. This chair *soll* have belonged to a duke. It *dürfte* be from around 1780. It *kann* be genuine, and it *muss* be sold by Friday. It’s the last chapter you’ll need on how sure you are.

grammar[0].fact: Newspapers will often break this rule, and they’ll print *mit Dr. Weber, die Leiterin*. You’re expected to notice. Your reader may not, but Dr. Brummer does, and he’s written to the paper about it, and there’s a good chance it’s in one of his 400 letters.

grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Duty or guess?
grammar[1].blocks[2].root.q: Is there a perfect infinitive (gesehen haben, gewesen sein)?
grammar[1].blocks[2].root.no.answer: a duty, or a guess about now
grammar[1].fact: *Er muss es wissen* can be a duty, or a guess, and only the context can tell. Good German writers avoid the problem, and a good reader doesn’t get stuck. Lawyers fight about it. If you’ve got to here, you can read an entire crime novel from the modal verbs alone.

document.intro: The real base of a real cup. This is what Herr Lorenz was looking at. The word here is *Kahla*, a town in Thuringia that has made porcelain since the 1840s. Nothing else is said. For an expert, that’s plenty.
document.fact: Many a collector’s disappointment begins with turning a cup over. Go to your kitchen and try it.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say each about the cup, with a modal verb.
reading.intro: After the last book, Max couldn’t rest. He has taken Frau Huber’s blue cup, secretly, to Herr Lorenz, a dealer in the old town, to be valued. She thinks he’s borrowed it to have the handle repaired. Herr Lorenz looks at it with a magnifying glass, and at Max with something else.
reading.photos[0].caption: Glocken: Eine davon soll einem Herzog gehört haben.
reading.fact: Vienna’s old porcelain factory marked its pieces with a shield on the base, and Thuringia really did produce a great deal of porcelain. An expert looks first at the bottom of anything. On German TV, *Bares für Rares* is an extremely popular show in which people have their finds valued. Many take the valuation badly.
